medical.title: Early retinal dopamine imbalance appears across two inherited eye disease models
medical.summary: A new study by researchers at the University of Eastern Finland (UEF) reports changes in the dopamine system of the retina during inherited retinal degeneration. Inherited retinal degenerations form a diverse group of genetic eye diseases that lead to vision impairment and blindness as retinal function progressively declines.

medical.title: Gene map reveals how transplanted stem cells repair damaged heart muscle
medical.summary: Researchers led by Assistant Professor Lynn Yap of the Lee Kong Chian School of Medicine at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, have uncovered new insights into how unspecialized cells, also known as stem cells, develop and mature into heart muscle cells. The findings could pave the way for new treatments for heart disease.

medical.title: Student-athletes report need for suicide prevention, training
medical.summary: A survey of college athletes found that nearly 40% reported having suicidal thoughts during their lifetime. Some 86% also said the NCAA should require mental health and suicide prevention training for all athletes. The University of Mississippi and Rutgers University recently worked together to survey 78 student-athletes across NCAA Division I, II and III universities regarding suicidal thoughts and prevention strategies. They published their findings in Behavioral Sciences.

medical.title: Bone marrow transplants offer surprising way to treat mitochondrial disease
medical.summary: Bone marrow transplants offer an unexpected way for diseased cells in the heart and brain to get replacement parts, a Stanford Medicine-led study has shown. The finding offers hope for the first effective treatment of mitochondrial disorders, a group of genetic diseases in which cells' motors, called mitochondria, are dysfunctional.

medical.title: Sugar exposure in early life linked to anxiety in adulthood
medical.summary: Exposure to sugar in the first 1,000 days of a child's life increases the risk of developing anxiety in adulthood, according to a new study from the University of Surrey published in Translational Psychiatry. Scientists also found that sugar intake early in life can affect brain development, with significant differences identified in 11 of the brain's 80 regions.

medical.title: Rare genetic variant identified as new cause of neurodevelopmental disorders
medical.summary: Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine and Texas Children's Hospital's Duncan Neurological Research Institute (Duncan NRI) have identified a rare genetic change that appears to cause a newly recognized neurodevelopmental disorder. The discovery provides families with a potential explanation for previously undiagnosed developmental challenges and reveals a biological pathway that could guide future treatment research.

medical.title: Smelling freshly brewed coffee briefly improves mood, small study suggests
medical.summary: For millions around the globe, a freshly brewed cup of coffee is a wake-up drink first thing in the morning and a pick-me-up during a long, tedious workday. Scientists now have clues that it might be more than just the boost from the psychoactive component, caffeine, that explains why we reach for that roasted-bean brew so often.

medical.title: Higher adolescent BMI linked to faster biological aging decades later
medical.summary: A study by the Faculty of Sport and Health Sciences at the University of Jyväskylä, Finland, found that a high adolescent body mass index (BMI) may be linked to accelerated biological aging in adulthood. The findings, published in the International Journal of Obesity, suggest that adolescents with a higher BMI may age biologically faster than others do.

medical.title: Blood vessel features in tumors may help predict patient survival in colorectal cancer
medical.summary: Tumors require a blood supply to grow and survive. The blood vessels that nourish tumors can have different characteristics across cancer types and could be connected to patient survival and outcomes. Researchers from Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute, the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, and Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health conducted a prospective cohort study using advanced imaging techniques to microscopically characterize colorectal tumor vessels.

medical.title: Rare pregnancy infections linked to autism
medical.summary: Infections that, in rare cases, can be transmitted from a pregnant woman to the fetus are linked to an increased risk of autism and intellectual disability in the child. This is shown by a study from Karolinska Institutet published in JAMA Pediatrics.

medical.title: Existing cancer drug may protect the heart during certain chemotherapy treatments
medical.summary: The chemotherapy agent doxorubicin is used successfully to treat a range of cancers but can, as a side effect, damage the heart muscle. Researchers at the Heidelberg Faculty of Medicine at Heidelberg University have now identified the molecular signaling pathway through which doxorubicin causes cardiac injury. They also discovered that SAHA (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid), a drug already approved for the treatment of certain cancers, attenuated harmful mechanisms in heart muscle cells in cell-based and animal studies and could therefore help protect the heart.

medical.title: Changes in oral anticoagulant and cardiovascular drug use with the progression of neurodegenerative disorders
medical.summary: Cardiovascular diseases are common among people living with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). Understanding drug utilization patterns in these populations is important for ensuring safe and effective treatment, supporting clinical decision-making and improving the overall care of people living with AD and PD. However, little is known about how the use of oral anticoagulants and cardiovascular drugs changes during the progression of these disorders.

medical.title: Twenty minutes of calming music offers health care workers a chance to recharge
medical.summary: While burnout in the medical field is well documented, affecting about half of health care workers, far fewer studies have explored ways to address it. A Northwestern Medicine study has found one simple intervention may help.

medical.title: Beyond raw brainpower: New study reveals best ways to train AI for clinical care
medical.summary: Harnessing generative AI to help doctors make critical medical decisions requires more than raw technology. A new review study in the Journal of Medical Internet Research shows that adapting existing language models is key to ensuring they can safely and effectively assist with clinical diagnoses, patient triage and treatment planning in real-world health care settings.

medical.title: Study links soaring health care spending to higher insurance premiums
medical.summary: Growth in health care spending in the United States is driving increases in health insurance premiums, limiting people's access to care and contributing to wage reductions, job losses and rising inequality, according to a new study co-authored by Yale economist Zack Cooper.

medical.title: Can nutrients in our foods mimic calorie restriction and increase our healthspan?
medical.summary: Scroll through social media and you will soon encounter advice about living longer, from fasting plans and supplements to elaborate daily routines. Yet reaching an advanced age tells us little about how healthy or independent those later years will be.

medical.title: Are girls getting their periods earlier? And can parents do anything about it?
medical.summary: Do you remember how old you were when you got your first period? And whether it was considered early, late or about average?

medical.title: Teen with extraordinary memory relives his past far more often than most people do
medical.summary: The human brain is a mystery that keeps unraveling, revealing something fascinating with every discovery. For years, scientists have been trying to better understand a rare condition called Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory (HSAM). People with HSAM can recall detailed personal experiences from across their lifetime with an unusually high level of accuracy and speed, without having to rely on memory techniques.

medical.title: Researchers seek a role for Ghana's traditional healers in breast cancer care
medical.summary: In Ghana and many African countries, traditional medicine practitioners and faith healers play a prominent role in patient care. These practitioners use herbal remedies, spiritual healing or other practices rooted in local customs or knowledge passed down through generations. Trusted by their communities, they are accessible, affordable and regarded as more patient-centered than conventional or orthodox health care.

medical.title: Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once
medical.summary: A new needle-thin brain implant can record neural activity, deliver drugs, and stimulate multiple brain regions using a single flexible fiber. Successful tests in mice suggest it could give scientists a more precise, less invasive way to study the brain and may eventually help treat neurological disorders such as epilepsy.

medical.title: Government-owned aged care homes linked to fewer hospital visits in Australia
medical.summary: Experts have raised concerns about a gradual shift in ownership and management models in Australia's aged care facilities—and the subsequent impact this has on the quality of care and resident health outcomes.

medical.title: Dementia survey finds caregivers overwhelmed as one-third provide 70 hours of care
medical.summary: New national survey findings show that while many Australians living with dementia report positive well-being and support from family and friends, the pathway to diagnosis can be complex and support services can be difficult to navigate.

medical.title: Promising AI tool to speed up endometriosis diagnosis
medical.summary: The AI tool, called "EndoFusion," is a recent development from IMAGENDOÒ, an ongoing collaborative study led by Adelaide University researchers. In this latest study, researchers found the framework could accurately identify two major indicators of advanced endometriosis in pelvic scans, producing results in just 18 milliseconds.

medical.title: Stanford scientists discover the human brain may actually be two separate organs
medical.summary: Scientists have found that the human brain develops from two distinct cellular systems, suggesting that evolution fused together two ancient nervous systems with very different jobs. The discovery also allowed researchers to grow human hindbrain neurons in the lab, opening new possibilities for studying ALS, spinal muscular atrophy, and other brainstem diseases.

medical.title: What happened when I stopped filling the silence
medical.summary: Angela Garwood swapped conversation for stillness at a device-free silent retreat, hoping to discover what lies beneath the noise The post What happened when I stopped filling the silence appeared first on Positive News .

science.title: Drought in the Northeastern United States has decreased
science.summary: As climate change continues to affect the U.S., many regions throughout the country, especially the West, are experiencing more drought.

science.title: Elusive builders of nearly perfect hexagonal tunnel fossils were probably small crustaceans—not worms
science.summary: For more than 170 years, paleontologists have been trying to solve the mystery of what created the strangely uniform hexagonal tunnels found in fossils. In a new study published in Earth Science Reviews, a team of researchers pored over the evidence and concluded that the most likely culprit was a type of arthropod—probably a small crustacean. This challenges a long-standing idea that a worm-like creature may have created the tunnels.

science.title: Under stress, bacterial RNA and proteins tell different stories
science.summary: During infection, bacteria encounter rapidly changing and stressful environments inside the body. To understand how they adapt, researchers often measure messenger RNA (mRNA), which carries information from genes that can be translated into proteins. While mRNA levels are widely used to monitor bacterial responses, proteins carry out much of the work inside the cell and are influenced by processes that occur after RNA has been produced.

science.title: Exploring the brain and behavior of children who struggle with math
science.summary: Some children have a condition that causes them to persistently struggle with math problem-solving (developmental dyscalculia), yet behavioral and mechanistic details about this condition are lacking.

science.title: Nuclear-spin swap extends room-temperature entanglement lifetime up to 240-fold
science.summary: Researchers in China have extended the lifetime of entanglement in a room-temperature, solid-state system by up to a factor of 240. Led by Shuo Ren and Rui-Jian Liang at the University of Science and Technology of China in Hefei, the team transferred entangled states from the electron spins of solid-state defects to the spins of surrounding atomic nuclei, which are far more resilient to noise. The research has been published in Physical Review Letters.

science.title: New tool helps responders identify highest-risk areas for post-hurricane rescue efforts
science.summary: Researchers have developed a mathematical model to predict which neighborhoods should be prioritized for search and rescue operations in the wake of a hurricane, with the goal of expediting recovery operations by the Coast Guard or other responders. The research is published in the International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction.

science.title: A mushroom-powered boost for soybean byproducts
science.summary: Scientists from Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) have demonstrated in a lab-scale study a fermentation method that could transform okara, a nutrient-rich soybean byproduct from tofu and soymilk production, into a more flavorful and protein-rich food ingredient.

science.title: Superdense neutron star caught feeding on a blue hypergiant's stellar wind
science.summary: Using data from the Japan–led XRISM (X-ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission) observatory, astronomers have directly observed a giant star's outflow, called a stellar wind, being captured by its compact companion and providing the power source for strong X-ray flares. The research is part of NASA's exploration of the extreme universe to better understand how the cosmos works.

science.title: Family interactions can help young beetles cope with climate stress, study finds
science.summary: Climate change is one of the most complex challenges of our time and places considerable strain on a wide range of animal groups. A research team at the University of Bayreuth has used burying beetles to investigate the extent to which social interactions among family members can buffer the effects of environmental stress.

science.title: Does Tutankhamen's tomb hold his stepmother Queen Nefertiti's remains? New study offers tantalizing clues
science.summary: When Tutankhamun's tomb was discovered over a century ago, it became an immediate worldwide sensation, revealing a wealth of treasures from ancient Egypt. In the decades that followed, the tomb was meticulously cleared, cataloged and studied, leading many to believe that KV 62, as it is officially known, had given up all its secrets. Yet long after its opening, the boy king's final resting place may still hold mysteries.

science.title: Scientists teleport quantum states across 100 parallel optical channels
science.summary: Quantum communication networks consist of several connected nodes that exchange information encoded in quantum states. These networks could potentially enable more secure communications between quantum devices in different locations.

science.title: AI is distorting archaeology and flattening Indigenous knowledge
science.summary: If you search Google Images for "cultural heritage Australia," near the top of the results is a photograph of giant carved stone heads rising from a red desert.

science.title: Q&A: Tiny spores for a big critical minerals challenge
science.summary: Scientists at the Department of Energy's (DOE) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) are exploring how durable, customizable bacterial spores could capture rare earth elements (REE) from acid mine drainage and other metal-containing waste streams. The project supports new methods of sourcing critical minerals essential for the nation's economic strength and national security.

science.title: A 'rebellious' exoplanet orbits in the opposite direction of its star
science.summary: A star and its planets form when a cloud of gas and dust collapses in on itself somewhere in space. The cloud then forms a disk around the nascent star, within which the planets will form. This protostar and its disk then rotate in the same direction.

science.title: End of humanity? Blow‑by‑blow account of what would happen if the Yellowstone supervolcano erupted now
science.summary: Around 631,000 years ago—a geological blink of an eye—catastrophe unfolded in what is now northwestern Wyoming, U.S. During what is thought to have been a series of immense volcanic eruptions, life within hundreds of kilometers of the blasts was shattered. Ash was dispersed across much of North America, and the effects were felt worldwide. This was a super-eruption of the massive volcanic system located in what is now Yellowstone National Park.

science.title: Living with chronic pain at work: Supportive managers can help, but they can't solve everything
science.summary: "I don't want the pain to define me. I want me to define me."

science.title: Environmental science takes an average of seven years to influence international policy, study finds
science.summary: A new study led by the University of Alicante (UA) and the Mediterranean Center for Environmental Studies (CEAM) analyzes the barriers separating scientific knowledge from environmental policy and its effective implementation. The research sets out how long it takes for scientific knowledge in ecology to reach environmental policies and the extent to which these policies subsequently translate into real-world outcomes.

science.title: The Red Planet has a purple side
science.summary: Oxidized iron dominates the Martian color palette. The dusty reds, ochers, browns and tans give the planet its nickname: the Red Planet. But new images of Mars' south polar region show something different. Swirls of pink, purple and red highlight the region and a feature named Thyles Rupes, an icy crag with cliffs higher than 1 km (0.6 miles). Rupes means cliff in Latin, while Thyles is a mythical northern land spoken of in the ancient world.

science.title: X-ray light is like guitar music, with frequencies sliding continuously between harmonics
science.summary: Ultrashort laser pulses can be used to generate X-rays. Normally, however, only certain specific frequencies are produced. A team from TU Wien and the University of California San Diego has developed a method that makes it possible to tune the frequency continuously.

science.title: Black holes of every size follow the same surprising rule
science.summary: Scientists have found evidence that black holes of vastly different sizes may launch powerful jets according to the same universal rule. Supermassive black holes can produce jets soon after tearing apart a star, then fire up again hundreds or thousands of days later when their feeding rate drops to about 2% of the Eddington limit. That same threshold is known to trigger jets from much smaller black holes in the Milky Way.

science.title: Flies, mice and humans share a walking pattern despite radically different bodies
science.summary: Flies, mice and humans move in different ways because of their very different physiques, but their movements follow a common pattern— joints farther from the center of the body move faster than those closer to the body. This was demonstrated in a study conducted by a research team from the University of Cologne and Forschungszentrum Jülich led by Professor Dr. Silvia Daun and Professor Dr. Graziana Gatto.

science.title: A new process turns plastic waste into gasoline and diesel fuel
science.summary: Scientists at Oak Ridge National Laboratory have developed a surprisingly simple way to turn polyethylene, the common plastic used in shopping bags and cutting boards, into gasoline and diesel-like fuels. The process uses inexpensive aluminum-based molten salts to break long plastic molecules into smaller hydrocarbons, producing about 60% gasoline under relatively mild conditions.

science.title: Tiny molecular scissors reveal how crystals bend without breaking
science.summary: Crystals are usually thought of as rigid and brittle. Yet some molecular crystals can bend, jump, twist or even change shape when exposed to light. Understanding how tiny molecular movements inside an ordered crystal can produce such large visible motions is an important challenge for developing responsive materials that could eventually be used in actuators, sensors and other miniature devices.

science.title: African smoke brightens clouds, but weather patterns offset its cooling effect
science.summary: Smoke from African agricultural fires brightens clouds over the southeast Atlantic—but new research from scientists at the University of Miami Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric and Earth Science shows that the same weather pattern carrying the smoke also thins clouds and reduces cloud cover, effectively offsetting its cooling effect.

science.title: School holidays are coming. Here's how families can keep some sort of routine
science.summary: School holidays mean more free time and less structure.

environment.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
environment.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

environment.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
environment.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

environment.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

environment.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
environment.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.title: Early retinal dopamine imbalance appears across two inherited eye disease models
mix_items.summary: A new study by researchers at the University of Eastern Finland (UEF) reports changes in the dopamine system of the retina during inherited retinal degeneration. Inherited retinal degenerations form a diverse group of genetic eye diseases that lead to vision impairment and blindness as retinal function progressively declines.

mix_items.title: Elusive builders of nearly perfect hexagonal tunnel fossils were probably small crustaceans—not worms
mix_items.summary: For more than 170 years, paleontologists have been trying to solve the mystery of what created the strangely uniform hexagonal tunnels found in fossils. In a new study published in Earth Science Reviews, a team of researchers pored over the evidence and concluded that the most likely culprit was a type of arthropod—probably a small crustacean. This challenges a long-standing idea that a worm-like creature may have created the tunnels.

mix_items.title: Under stress, bacterial RNA and proteins tell different stories
mix_items.summary: During infection, bacteria encounter rapidly changing and stressful environments inside the body. To understand how they adapt, researchers often measure messenger RNA (mRNA), which carries information from genes that can be translated into proteins. While mRNA levels are widely used to monitor bacterial responses, proteins carry out much of the work inside the cell and are influenced by processes that occur after RNA has been produced.

mix_items.title: Gene map reveals how transplanted stem cells repair damaged heart muscle
mix_items.summary: Researchers led by Assistant Professor Lynn Yap of the Lee Kong Chian School of Medicine at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, have uncovered new insights into how unspecialized cells, also known as stem cells, develop and mature into heart muscle cells. The findings could pave the way for new treatments for heart disease.

mix_items.title: Student-athletes report need for suicide prevention, training
mix_items.summary: A survey of college athletes found that nearly 40% reported having suicidal thoughts during their lifetime. Some 86% also said the NCAA should require mental health and suicide prevention training for all athletes. The University of Mississippi and Rutgers University recently worked together to survey 78 student-athletes across NCAA Division I, II and III universities regarding suicidal thoughts and prevention strategies. They published their findings in Behavioral Sciences.

mix_items.title: Exploring the brain and behavior of children who struggle with math
mix_items.summary: Some children have a condition that causes them to persistently struggle with math problem-solving (developmental dyscalculia), yet behavioral and mechanistic details about this condition are lacking.

mix_items.title: Bone marrow transplants offer surprising way to treat mitochondrial disease
mix_items.summary: Bone marrow transplants offer an unexpected way for diseased cells in the heart and brain to get replacement parts, a Stanford Medicine-led study has shown. The finding offers hope for the first effective treatment of mitochondrial disorders, a group of genetic diseases in which cells' motors, called mitochondria, are dysfunctional.

mix_items.title: Nuclear-spin swap extends room-temperature entanglement lifetime up to 240-fold
mix_items.summary: Researchers in China have extended the lifetime of entanglement in a room-temperature, solid-state system by up to a factor of 240. Led by Shuo Ren and Rui-Jian Liang at the University of Science and Technology of China in Hefei, the team transferred entangled states from the electron spins of solid-state defects to the spins of surrounding atomic nuclei, which are far more resilient to noise. The research has been published in Physical Review Letters.

mix_items.title: New tool helps responders identify highest-risk areas for post-hurricane rescue efforts
mix_items.summary: Researchers have developed a mathematical model to predict which neighborhoods should be prioritized for search and rescue operations in the wake of a hurricane, with the goal of expediting recovery operations by the Coast Guard or other responders. The research is published in the International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction.

mix_items.title: Sugar exposure in early life linked to anxiety in adulthood
mix_items.summary: Exposure to sugar in the first 1,000 days of a child's life increases the risk of developing anxiety in adulthood, according to a new study from the University of Surrey published in Translational Psychiatry. Scientists also found that sugar intake early in life can affect brain development, with significant differences identified in 11 of the brain's 80 regions.

mix_items.title: A mushroom-powered boost for soybean byproducts
mix_items.summary: Scientists from Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) have demonstrated in a lab-scale study a fermentation method that could transform okara, a nutrient-rich soybean byproduct from tofu and soymilk production, into a more flavorful and protein-rich food ingredient.

mix_items.title: Rare genetic variant identified as new cause of neurodevelopmental disorders
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine and Texas Children's Hospital's Duncan Neurological Research Institute (Duncan NRI) have identified a rare genetic change that appears to cause a newly recognized neurodevelopmental disorder. The discovery provides families with a potential explanation for previously undiagnosed developmental challenges and reveals a biological pathway that could guide future treatment research.

mix_items.title: Superdense neutron star caught feeding on a blue hypergiant's stellar wind
mix_items.summary: Using data from the Japan–led XRISM (X-ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission) observatory, astronomers have directly observed a giant star's outflow, called a stellar wind, being captured by its compact companion and providing the power source for strong X-ray flares. The research is part of NASA's exploration of the extreme universe to better understand how the cosmos works.

mix_items.title: Family interactions can help young beetles cope with climate stress, study finds
mix_items.summary: Climate change is one of the most complex challenges of our time and places considerable strain on a wide range of animal groups. A research team at the University of Bayreuth has used burying beetles to investigate the extent to which social interactions among family members can buffer the effects of environmental stress.

mix_items.title: Smelling freshly brewed coffee briefly improves mood, small study suggests
mix_items.summary: For millions around the globe, a freshly brewed cup of coffee is a wake-up drink first thing in the morning and a pick-me-up during a long, tedious workday. Scientists now have clues that it might be more than just the boost from the psychoactive component, caffeine, that explains why we reach for that roasted-bean brew so often.

mix_items.title: Higher adolescent BMI linked to faster biological aging decades later
mix_items.summary: A study by the Faculty of Sport and Health Sciences at the University of Jyväskylä, Finland, found that a high adolescent body mass index (BMI) may be linked to accelerated biological aging in adulthood. The findings, published in the International Journal of Obesity, suggest that adolescents with a higher BMI may age biologically faster than others do.

mix_items.title: Does Tutankhamen's tomb hold his stepmother Queen Nefertiti's remains? New study offers tantalizing clues
mix_items.summary: When Tutankhamun's tomb was discovered over a century ago, it became an immediate worldwide sensation, revealing a wealth of treasures from ancient Egypt. In the decades that followed, the tomb was meticulously cleared, cataloged and studied, leading many to believe that KV 62, as it is officially known, had given up all its secrets. Yet long after its opening, the boy king's final resting place may still hold mysteries.

mix_items.title: Scientists teleport quantum states across 100 parallel optical channels
mix_items.summary: Quantum communication networks consist of several connected nodes that exchange information encoded in quantum states. These networks could potentially enable more secure communications between quantum devices in different locations.

mix_items.title: AI is distorting archaeology and flattening Indigenous knowledge
mix_items.summary: If you search Google Images for "cultural heritage Australia," near the top of the results is a photograph of giant carved stone heads rising from a red desert.

mix_items.title: Blood vessel features in tumors may help predict patient survival in colorectal cancer
mix_items.summary: Tumors require a blood supply to grow and survive. The blood vessels that nourish tumors can have different characteristics across cancer types and could be connected to patient survival and outcomes. Researchers from Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute, the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, and Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health conducted a prospective cohort study using advanced imaging techniques to microscopically characterize colorectal tumor vessels.

mix_items.title: Q&A: Tiny spores for a big critical minerals challenge
mix_items.summary: Scientists at the Department of Energy's (DOE) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) are exploring how durable, customizable bacterial spores could capture rare earth elements (REE) from acid mine drainage and other metal-containing waste streams. The project supports new methods of sourcing critical minerals essential for the nation's economic strength and national security.

mix_items.title: Rare pregnancy infections linked to autism
mix_items.summary: Infections that, in rare cases, can be transmitted from a pregnant woman to the fetus are linked to an increased risk of autism and intellectual disability in the child. This is shown by a study from Karolinska Institutet published in JAMA Pediatrics.

mix_items.title: A 'rebellious' exoplanet orbits in the opposite direction of its star
mix_items.summary: A star and its planets form when a cloud of gas and dust collapses in on itself somewhere in space. The cloud then forms a disk around the nascent star, within which the planets will form. This protostar and its disk then rotate in the same direction.

mix_items.title: Existing cancer drug may protect the heart during certain chemotherapy treatments
mix_items.summary: The chemotherapy agent doxorubicin is used successfully to treat a range of cancers but can, as a side effect, damage the heart muscle. Researchers at the Heidelberg Faculty of Medicine at Heidelberg University have now identified the molecular signaling pathway through which doxorubicin causes cardiac injury. They also discovered that SAHA (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid), a drug already approved for the treatment of certain cancers, attenuated harmful mechanisms in heart muscle cells in cell-based and animal studies and could therefore help protect the heart.

mix_items.title: End of humanity? Blow‑by‑blow account of what would happen if the Yellowstone supervolcano erupted now
mix_items.summary: Around 631,000 years ago—a geological blink of an eye—catastrophe unfolded in what is now northwestern Wyoming, U.S. During what is thought to have been a series of immense volcanic eruptions, life within hundreds of kilometers of the blasts was shattered. Ash was dispersed across much of North America, and the effects were felt worldwide. This was a super-eruption of the massive volcanic system located in what is now Yellowstone National Park.

mix_items.title: Changes in oral anticoagulant and cardiovascular drug use with the progression of neurodegenerative disorders
mix_items.summary: Cardiovascular diseases are common among people living with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). Understanding drug utilization patterns in these populations is important for ensuring safe and effective treatment, supporting clinical decision-making and improving the overall care of people living with AD and PD. However, little is known about how the use of oral anticoagulants and cardiovascular drugs changes during the progression of these disorders.

mix_items.title: Living with chronic pain at work: Supportive managers can help, but they can't solve everything
mix_items.summary: "I don't want the pain to define me. I want me to define me."

mix_items.title: Twenty minutes of calming music offers health care workers a chance to recharge
mix_items.summary: While burnout in the medical field is well documented, affecting about half of health care workers, far fewer studies have explored ways to address it. A Northwestern Medicine study has found one simple intervention may help.

mix_items.title: Environmental science takes an average of seven years to influence international policy, study finds
mix_items.summary: A new study led by the University of Alicante (UA) and the Mediterranean Center for Environmental Studies (CEAM) analyzes the barriers separating scientific knowledge from environmental policy and its effective implementation. The research sets out how long it takes for scientific knowledge in ecology to reach environmental policies and the extent to which these policies subsequently translate into real-world outcomes.

mix_items.title: Beyond raw brainpower: New study reveals best ways to train AI for clinical care
mix_items.summary: Harnessing generative AI to help doctors make critical medical decisions requires more than raw technology. A new review study in the Journal of Medical Internet Research shows that adapting existing language models is key to ensuring they can safely and effectively assist with clinical diagnoses, patient triage and treatment planning in real-world health care settings.

mix_items.title: The Red Planet has a purple side
mix_items.summary: Oxidized iron dominates the Martian color palette. The dusty reds, ochers, browns and tans give the planet its nickname: the Red Planet. But new images of Mars' south polar region show something different. Swirls of pink, purple and red highlight the region and a feature named Thyles Rupes, an icy crag with cliffs higher than 1 km (0.6 miles). Rupes means cliff in Latin, while Thyles is a mythical northern land spoken of in the ancient world.

mix_items.title: X-ray light is like guitar music, with frequencies sliding continuously between harmonics
mix_items.summary: Ultrashort laser pulses can be used to generate X-rays. Normally, however, only certain specific frequencies are produced. A team from TU Wien and the University of California San Diego has developed a method that makes it possible to tune the frequency continuously.

mix_items.title: Study links soaring health care spending to higher insurance premiums
mix_items.summary: Growth in health care spending in the United States is driving increases in health insurance premiums, limiting people's access to care and contributing to wage reductions, job losses and rising inequality, according to a new study co-authored by Yale economist Zack Cooper.

mix_items.title: Can nutrients in our foods mimic calorie restriction and increase our healthspan?
mix_items.summary: Scroll through social media and you will soon encounter advice about living longer, from fasting plans and supplements to elaborate daily routines. Yet reaching an advanced age tells us little about how healthy or independent those later years will be.

mix_items.title: Black holes of every size follow the same surprising rule
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found evidence that black holes of vastly different sizes may launch powerful jets according to the same universal rule. Supermassive black holes can produce jets soon after tearing apart a star, then fire up again hundreds or thousands of days later when their feeding rate drops to about 2% of the Eddington limit. That same threshold is known to trigger jets from much smaller black holes in the Milky Way.

mix_items.title: Flies, mice and humans share a walking pattern despite radically different bodies
mix_items.summary: Flies, mice and humans move in different ways because of their very different physiques, but their movements follow a common pattern— joints farther from the center of the body move faster than those closer to the body. This was demonstrated in a study conducted by a research team from the University of Cologne and Forschungszentrum Jülich led by Professor Dr. Silvia Daun and Professor Dr. Graziana Gatto.

mix_items.title: Are girls getting their periods earlier? And can parents do anything about it?
mix_items.summary: Do you remember how old you were when you got your first period? And whether it was considered early, late or about average?

mix_items.title: A new process turns plastic waste into gasoline and diesel fuel
mix_items.summary: Scientists at Oak Ridge National Laboratory have developed a surprisingly simple way to turn polyethylene, the common plastic used in shopping bags and cutting boards, into gasoline and diesel-like fuels. The process uses inexpensive aluminum-based molten salts to break long plastic molecules into smaller hydrocarbons, producing about 60% gasoline under relatively mild conditions.

mix_items.title: Teen with extraordinary memory relives his past far more often than most people do
mix_items.summary: The human brain is a mystery that keeps unraveling, revealing something fascinating with every discovery. For years, scientists have been trying to better understand a rare condition called Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory (HSAM). People with HSAM can recall detailed personal experiences from across their lifetime with an unusually high level of accuracy and speed, without having to rely on memory techniques.

mix_items.title: Tiny molecular scissors reveal how crystals bend without breaking
mix_items.summary: Crystals are usually thought of as rigid and brittle. Yet some molecular crystals can bend, jump, twist or even change shape when exposed to light. Understanding how tiny molecular movements inside an ordered crystal can produce such large visible motions is an important challenge for developing responsive materials that could eventually be used in actuators, sensors and other miniature devices.

mix_items.title: Researchers seek a role for Ghana's traditional healers in breast cancer care
mix_items.summary: In Ghana and many African countries, traditional medicine practitioners and faith healers play a prominent role in patient care. These practitioners use herbal remedies, spiritual healing or other practices rooted in local customs or knowledge passed down through generations. Trusted by their communities, they are accessible, affordable and regarded as more patient-centered than conventional or orthodox health care.

mix_items.title: African smoke brightens clouds, but weather patterns offset its cooling effect
mix_items.summary: Smoke from African agricultural fires brightens clouds over the southeast Atlantic—but new research from scientists at the University of Miami Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric and Earth Science shows that the same weather pattern carrying the smoke also thins clouds and reduces cloud cover, effectively offsetting its cooling effect.

mix_items.title: School holidays are coming. Here's how families can keep some sort of routine
mix_items.summary: School holidays mean more free time and less structure.

mix_items.title: Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once
mix_items.summary: A new needle-thin brain implant can record neural activity, deliver drugs, and stimulate multiple brain regions using a single flexible fiber. Successful tests in mice suggest it could give scientists a more precise, less invasive way to study the brain and may eventually help treat neurological disorders such as epilepsy.

mix_items.title: Government-owned aged care homes linked to fewer hospital visits in Australia
mix_items.summary: Experts have raised concerns about a gradual shift in ownership and management models in Australia's aged care facilities—and the subsequent impact this has on the quality of care and resident health outcomes.

mix_items.title: Dementia survey finds caregivers overwhelmed as one-third provide 70 hours of care
mix_items.summary: New national survey findings show that while many Australians living with dementia report positive well-being and support from family and friends, the pathway to diagnosis can be complex and support services can be difficult to navigate.

mix_items.title: Promising AI tool to speed up endometriosis diagnosis
mix_items.summary: The AI tool, called "EndoFusion," is a recent development from IMAGENDOÒ, an ongoing collaborative study led by Adelaide University researchers. In this latest study, researchers found the framework could accurately identify two major indicators of advanced endometriosis in pelvic scans, producing results in just 18 milliseconds.

mix_items.title: Stanford scientists discover the human brain may actually be two separate organs
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found that the human brain develops from two distinct cellular systems, suggesting that evolution fused together two ancient nervous systems with very different jobs. The discovery also allowed researchers to grow human hindbrain neurons in the lab, opening new possibilities for studying ALS, spinal muscular atrophy, and other brainstem diseases.

mix_items.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
mix_items.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

mix_items.title: What happened when I stopped filling the silence
mix_items.summary: Angela Garwood swapped conversation for stillness at a device-free silent retreat, hoping to discover what lies beneath the noise The post What happened when I stopped filling the silence appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
mix_items.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

mix_items.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
mix_items.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
